unconjugated (indirect > direct) hyperbilirubinemia in the first week of life that is caused by insufficient

Episodic crying, abdominal tenderness, and lethargy suggest intussusception, an intestinal emergency
most common in children age 6-36 months. Intussusception occurs when a segment of bowel telescopes
into an adjacent segment. Intermittent contraction of the telescoped bowel during peristalsis results in the
classic presentation of episodic inconsolable crying with legs flexed and drawn into the abdomen,
followed by asymptomatic periods of normal activity. Increasing lethargy occurs with progressive
episodes and, in a minority of cases, may be the presenting sign (particularly in infants).

Early detection is critical to avoid bowel obstruction and ischemia of the involved segment (ie, bloody
currant jelly stool). Examination may reveal abdominal tenderness or a sausage-shaped abdominal mass
but is often normal. The first step in management of suspected intussusception is abdominal ultrasound,
which reveals the telescoped intestine as a target sign, or two concentric circles. Abdominal x-ray may
also be performed to exclude intestinal perforation that would warrant surgical management.

Air (or saline) enema is the treatment of choice to reduce intussusception nonsurgically.
educationalObjective: Intussusception is an abdominal emergency. Affected patients have episodes of inconsolable crying, with legs drawn to the abdomen due to pain, followed by asymptomatic periods. the most common gastrointestinal congenital anomaly. Meckel diverticulum results from a partial remnant
of the fetal vitelline duct, an embryologic structure that typically obliterates in the first trimester. A Meckel
diverticulum may contain ectopic gastric mucosa (or, less commonly, pancreatic tissue), which secretes

may lead to pallor and anemia if chronic, as in this case. Stools can range in color from dark red or maroon
to black depending on colonic transit time; the latter is more common in adults. Abdominal pain, diarrhea,
and vomiting are uncommon.

The best diagnostic test is a technetium-99m pertechnetate scan (Meckel scan), which shows increased
uptake of technetium-99m by gastric mucosa and therefore identifies ectopic gastric tissue. This test is
noninvasive, highly sensitive and specific, and emits little radiation. In symptomatic patients, surgical
resection is necessary to prevent further bleeding or other complications (eg, intussusception, obstruction).
